text: You'll see thousands of pumpkins tonight, but the first jack-o'-lanterns were never pumpkins,
so what were they? Turnips. And it all started on one small hill in Ireland.
So how did an Irish turnip end up on every American porch? Rewind.
County Meath, Ireland. The hill of Ward, once called Tlachta. People may have gathered here
since about 1000 BC. Old Irish texts link it to Samhain, the end of harvest, the start
of winter, on the night of the 31st of October. The story goes, a great fire was lit here,
and torches carried it to hills across the land. That night, spirits were said to walk,
so people carved scary faces into turnips. Why is it always me? Then, in the 1800s,
Irish immigrants crossed the Atlantic to America.
They brought the tradition, but America had something better than turnips.
Pumpkins. Bigger, softer, and way easier to carve.
Finally, a job I'm good at.
This year, Americans are expected to spend about $13.5 billion on Halloween.
So the world's spookiest night began as a bonfire on one quiet Irish hill.
I was here first. Remember that.
